Dear Swati,
I'm sorry I missed your engagement. I know you set a place for me. The centre had a retreat that weekend and it's important I don't miss those now. You'll understand one day.
I know it's been months. Things are busy. We're at the centre most evenings, and weekends too. I gave some of my scholarship money to the building fund in March; it felt right after everything they've given me. Then the course fees went up, and I thought, I've already come so far, why stop now?
I can't really explain what we do. We're asked not to discuss it with people outside. It's not secret, exactly. It's just private.
My phone stays with the coordinator during sessions, so if I don't reply, that's why.
Please don't tell Mummy I wrote. She'll only worry.
With love, always,
Neelam

qa.q: What did Neelam give some of the scholarship money to?
qa.a: Neelam gave some of the scholarship money to the building fund in March.

qa.q: What does Neelam's line 'I've already come so far, why stop now?' reveal?
qa.a: It shows that the sacrifices already made are pushing Neelam to accept the next demand, even while feeling unsure.

qa.q: What would be a wise step for Swati after reading this letter?
qa.a: Swati could reply warmly, keep the door open, and quietly seek advice from a trusted adult or counsellor rather than keep this from Neelam's family.

qa.q: How might Swati feel reading 'please don't tell Mummy'?
qa.a: Swati may feel torn and worried, since the request for secrecy is itself a sign that Neelam is being cut off from family.

grounding: It shows a young person giving more time, money and secrecy to a group while contact with family falls, each step small and justified by past sacrifice.

I'm Manjula. From outside it looks like one big jump. It wasn't.
First, Lokesh sir asked me to come to Sunday meetings. Then Wednesdays too. Then he said my phone should stay off during study hours, so my sister's calls went unanswered. Then a small donation, then a bigger one for the retreat. Then he said, "Don't discuss our teachings with outsiders; they'll twist them." So I stopped telling my college friend Anju what I did at weekends. Soon I stopped seeing Anju at all.
Every step was tiny. And every time I hesitated, I thought of everything I'd already given, the money, the months, the friends. How could I stop now and make all of it pointless?
By the end of that year I was in the hall five nights a week and hadn't been home in four months. I only saw it clearly when my sister turned up at the hostel gate and cried.

qa.q: What did Lokesh sir say about outsiders?
qa.a: Don't discuss our teachings with outsiders; they'll twist them.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling each time a new step felt hard?
qa.a: Manjula felt uneasy and trapped by past sacrifice, afraid that stopping would make everything already given pointless.

qa.q: What turning point appears in the story?
qa.a: The sister turning up at the hostel gate and crying; a family member's loving, direct presence broke through the isolation.

qa.q: How might Anju have experienced Manjula's disappearance?
qa.a: Anju probably felt confused and hurt, losing a friend step by step without knowing why.

grounding: A young adult recalls small, rising demands for time, money and secrecy that cut off family and friends, each step made necessary by the last.

College counsellor's note, 3 September
Payal, a second-year, came to me this morning worried about her friend Sumit. She said he joined a "leadership circle" off campus. Now he attends four nights a week, has paid for two "advanced levels" out of his hostel fees, and has been told not to discuss the circle with anyone who "hasn't committed". He stopped replying to Payal after she questioned it, and his roommate says he hasn't called home in a month.
I met Sumit at noon. He was polite but guarded. He said, "I've already put in so much, it would be stupid to stop now." He looked exhausted.
I told him he was not in trouble, that he could talk to me any time, and asked if he would call his parents with me. He agreed to a call this evening. I have also informed the warden and the dean of students, and I will check in with Payal tomorrow.

qa.q: How many nights a week does Sumit attend the circle?
qa.a: Four nights a week.

qa.q: What does Sumit's remark about having put in so much suggest he feels?
qa.a: He feels trapped and exhausted, afraid that stopping would waste everything he has already given.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do, and why does it matter?
qa.a: The counsellor met Sumit the same day without blaming him, arranged a call with his parents that evening, and told the warden and dean, so he isn't left alone in it.

qa.q: What is it like for Payal to see Sumit change?
qa.a: Payal feels worried and shut out, losing contact after questioning the circle and unsure how to help.

grounding: A counsellor notes a student whose group demands more time, money and secrecy while contact with dissenting friends and family falls away.

Charu's diary, Tuesday night
Skipped the second half of my lab again because Sister Meenal said the evening session "needs everyone." Last month it was just Sundays. Now it's Tuesdays, Thursdays and Sunday, and the monthly contribution went up again. I told myself it's fine, I've already given so much that stopping now would waste it.
Damini called twice today. I didn't pick up. Sister Meenal says people from our old college "drain energy" and it's better not to explain the group to them. I haven't told Mum about the contributions either. It feels like a small thing each time.
Damini sent: "Miss you. Are you okay? No lecture, promise." I read it three times.
Tomorrow's session is at six. My attendance at college is below the limit now. I don't know when that happened. I'm so tired.

qa.q: Which days does Charu now go to the group's sessions?
qa.a: Charu now goes on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Sunday.

qa.q: What does reading Damini's message three times suggest about Charu?
qa.a: It suggests Charu feels lonely and torn, missing Damini even while the group tells Charu to stay away from old friends.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Charu tonight?
qa.a: Charu could reply to Damini, since Damini promised no lecture, and speak to her mum or a college counsellor about the rising time, money and secrecy.

qa.q: How might Damini be feeling when her calls go unanswered?
qa.a: Damini is probably worried and a little frightened, sensing Charu is slipping away but choosing to stay gentle so the door stays open.
